title: Certification from Examples is Hard for Circuits and Transformers under Minimal Overparametrization
claim: Adding one extra gate to a circuit lets it override the output on a trigger input while leaving all other behavior unchanged.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, red dashed additions highlight the modified circuit
description: Two side-by-side rounded panels each draw a layered threshold circuit. Inputs x1 to x4 sit at the bottom as circles. Above them is a row of four black 'Thr' gate circles, then a single top 'Thr' gate that outputs f*(x). The left panel shows the original circuit. The right panel repeats the same circuit and adds one red dashed 'Thr' gate, labeled CHECK_{I,π}(x) with I ⊆ [4], wired by red edges to all four inputs. A red edge also feeds this gate into the top gate, which is drawn in red dashed outline. A piecewise formula g_π(x) gives σ_π if CHECK_{I,π}(x)=1 and f*(x) otherwise. The eye goes first to the red additions on the right.
caption: Same-depth deceiver construction in $\TCzero$. Left: the original threshold circuit computing $f^\star$. Right: one additional threshold gate $\mathrm{CHECK}_{I,\pi}$ detects the trigger block and feeds the top threshold, which forces the output on that block while leaving the circuit unchanged elsewhere.
abstract: As state-of-the-art neural networks are deployed on reasoning and algorithmic tasks, exactness guarantees become increasingly important. However, high average-case accuracy can still mask incorrect behaviors. This motivates exact certification, which asks for the smallest set of labeled examples needed to certify that a learned hypothesis equals the target. We show that while some hypotheses are easy to certify, even minimal overparametrization can make certification exponentially hard across several hypothesis classes. For threshold circuits of depth $\ge 2$, adding a single extra gate can force certificate sizes exponential in the input dimension. We show an analogous hardness result for log-precision Transformers with only constant architectural overhead. We also characterize approximate certification, showing that allowing only polynomially many mistakes still requires exponentially large certificates, whereas constant relative-error guarantees can hide exponentially many failures. Empirically, we study binary-addition recognition using threshold circuits and Transformers trained with strong supervision. We find that incorrect models can survive extensive checks, with errors that often occur on different inputs and are difficult to detect through uniform sampling.
